chokepoint.physics: Separating 15+ chemically-alike elements is a vast solvent-extraction industrial base — ~85% China, gating the whole basket, not just magnets

eyebrow: Product-chain pilot · seventeen elements, one chokepoint
h1: Rare earths are not rare — separating them is the whole game
deck: The seventeen rare-earth elements are not scarce in the ground; they are just chemically near-identical and always found mixed together. Turning a mixed ore into pure, single-element oxides takes long solvent-extraction cascades — an industrial base that is roughly 85% China. That separation step gates not only magnets, but phosphors, polishing powders and refining catalysts alike.
byline: mixed ore (~70% China) ≠ separation (~85% China) ≠ Nd/Dy magnets · Eu/Tb phosphors · Ce polishing · La catalysts
correction: The magnet chain covers the neodymium and dysprosium story; this one is the whole basket. Rare earths are common in the crust — the difficulty is that the elements behave almost identically, so separating them into pure oxides is the hard, dirty, capital-heavy step, and it is ~85% China. That single capability gates every rare-earth product at once: magnets, the red and green phosphors in displays and lamps, cerium glass-polishing powder, and the lanthanum catalysts that crack crude oil.

sections.h2: 1 · The chokepoint is separation, not mining

panels.text: Rare earths come out of the ground as a mixture, and because the elements are chemically alike, pulling them apart into pure single-element oxides needs long solvent-extraction cascades, large reagent flows and the environmental permitting that comes with them. That industrial base sits roughly 85% in China. A mine in Australia or the US does not solve it — the ore still has to be separated, and separation is the bottleneck for everything downstream.

The 'light' rare earths (lanthanum, cerium, neodymium) are more abundant; the 'heavy' ones (dysprosium, terbium, yttrium) are scarcer and their separation is even more concentrated in China. So the parts of the basket that matter most for high-performance magnets and phosphors are exactly the parts with the thinnest alternative supply — which is what China's 2025 export licensing targeted.

cards.d: Nd, Pr, Dy, Tb → NdFeB permanent magnets — the largest and most strategic use (see the magnet chain).
Eu/Tb/Y give the colours in displays and LED lighting; cerium oxide polishes glass and chips.
Lanthanum-based catalysts crack crude oil in refineries; cerium aids autocatalysts — the quiet industrial uses.

panels.text: New mines are being opened outside China (Mountain Pass in the US, Mount Weld in Australia, plus Myanmar feedstock), but building non-Chinese separation capacity — the actual chokepoint — is slow, capital-heavy and environmentally fraught. It is a built capability, so it can be rebuilt; but on a timescale of years, which is why rare-earth security remains a live concern across magnets, electronics and defence.
